title: Spain Nears New India Co-Production Pact as It Wraps Country of Honor Run at IFFI Goa, WAVES Film Bazaar
description: Spain and India have moved closer to a fresh film and audiovisual co-production treaty as Spain wrapped its run as Country of Honor at the 57th Int
body:
Spain and India have moved closer to a fresh film and audiovisual co-production treaty as Spain wrapped its run as Country of Honor at the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI) in Goa and its market, WAVES Film Bazaar.

	On Nov. 21, Marta Serrano, director general of Spain’s Institute of Cinematography and Audiovisual Arts (ICAA), took the Spanish side into a bilateral meeting with India’s Ministry of Information and Broadcasting, whose team was fronted by Prithul Kumar, joint secretary for broadcasting and administration. Representatives of India Cine Hub also joined. The talks pushed forward negotiations on a pact to replace the treaty the two countries signed in 2012.
	

	Spain Film Commission, the non-profit umbrella group for Spain’s film commissions and film offices, organized the Spanish program in Goa alongside ICAA, which sits under the Ministry of Culture. ICEX–Invest in Spain and Casa de la India provided support. Funding came from the Ministry of Culture and from the Ministry for Digital Transformation and Public Administration, via its Secretary of State for Digitalization and Artificial Intelligence (SEDIA), under the Spain Audiovisual Hub Plan.

	“Our participation in IFFI Goa is part of a collaboration strategy that we have been developing with the Indian audiovisual industry for several years. Spain’s recognition as Country of Honor at this edition represents an important milestone, reflecting this collective effort and our close cooperation with ICAA and the other institutions involved. At Spain Film Commission, we will continue to promote these partnerships to create new opportunities for co-production, investment and filming across Spain’s territories,” said Juan Manuel Guimeráns, president of Spain Film Commission.
	

	The commission and ICAA had backed Spain’s bid for the honor in 2025, and the slot formed part of the Spain–India Dual Year of Culture, Tourism and Artificial Intelligence. Serrano’s team also included Camilo Vázquez, deputy director general for promotion and international relations, and technical adviser Irene López. Spain Film Commission sent general coordinator Lara Molina and communications director Raquel Alonso.

	At WAVES Film Bazaar, which ran Nov. 20–24, five production outfits chosen by ICAA – Federation Studios Spain, Pecado Films, Capitán Araña, Acortes Films and ESCAC Studio – pitched their projects and met prospective international partners.

	Spanish Day on Nov. 22 featured the panel “Spain: Where Stories Find Their Stage – Incentives, Locations & Co-Production Opportunities,” which made the case for Spain as a shooting destination and co-production partner. Vázquez and Molina were joined by Usha Jadhav of Acortes Films, Miguel Fabián Salazar of ICEX and Guillermo Rodríguez of Casa de la India. Spain Film Commission pointed to the country’s tax incentives, range of locations, crews and production facilities, plus the support its countrywide network gives visiting shoots. The session also showcased five Spanish projects seeking Indian partners, among them “The Dragon Letter,” Ladakh-born director Stanzin Jigmet’s project based on his Student Academy Award-winning short of the same name, and “Serendipia,” an India-Mexico-Spain romance.

	The commission also helped run a Spanish Networking Night that drew more than 200 guests. Among them were Indian ministry officials Prabhat, additional secretary; Kumar; and K.K. Nirala, joint secretary for institutions.

	On the festival side, IFFI’s Spanish selection included the world premiere of Juana Macías’ “Looking for Michael” (“Persiguiendo a Michael”), Pedro Almodóvar’s “Amarga Navidad,” Jaime Lorente’s “El mal hijo” and “Trinidad,” from Laura Alvea and José Ortuño.

	The delegation also attended screenings of Anna Saura’s documentary “Carlos Saura. Ese niño de la fotografía” and “Mudras. Bailando hilos invisibles,” directed by María Salgado Gispert and produced by Anna Saura, Marino García and Bobby Bedi. That film is the first official co-production between the two countries under the 2012 treaty.
	

	The Goa push comes as Spain Film Commission, founded in 2001, marks its 25th anniversary.

schema.headline: Spain Nears New India Co-Production Pact as It Wraps Country of Honor Run at IFFI Goa, WAVES Film Bazaar

title: South African President Cyril Ramaphosa Gives Speech at Canal+ Academy Training Program Launch: ‘You Are Living My Dream’
description: South African President Cyril Ramaphosa on Friday attended the launch of French media giant Canal+ Group’s Canal+ Academy at MultiChoice City in Jo
body:
South African President Cyril Ramaphosa on Friday attended the launch of French media giant Canal+ Group’s Canal+ Academy at MultiChoice City in Johannesburg. The new pan-African initiative will expand training and professional development opportunities for local aspiring professionals in the creative industries.

	The momentous event — which saw South Africa‘s leader, Canal+ CEO Maxime Saada and other top level executives delivering passionate speeches on the podium — comes after the company’s $2 billion takeover last year of South African pay TV company MultiChoice, which has made Canal+ the dominant player in Africa’s fast-growing pay TV market.
	

	Ramaphosa praised Canal+’s investment in MultiChoice and its decision to make the country an African media market hub, while also lauding the academy as a way to build Africa’s film and TV industry and expand opportunities for young people. 

	“Today, we are celebrating a significant moment in the country’s broadcasting and creative industries,” Ramaphosa said, adding: “I am very envious, because in my private life I’ve often said that one day I’d like to produce a movie.” 

	He quipped, “What I’m doing currently, it’s OK. But now, you are living my dream.”

	South Africa is becoming the first market to introduce the Canal + Academy model. The program, which incorporates the existing MultiChoice Talent Factory, aims to reach between 800 and 1,000 beneficiaries during its first 12 months.

	“For Canal+, Africa lies at the very heart of our strategy,” said Saada, noting that: “Today, we are a bi-continental group as deeply African as we are European.” He went on to proudly point out that the company behind “Paddington” is the only entertainment group listed on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange and underlined that “Canal+ Academy is a testament to this faith in Africa.”
	

	Saada then provided President Ramaphosa and the packed MultiChoice City auditorium a sneak peak of upcoming South Africa-set StudioCanal movie “The Road Home.” Directed by Bill Condon, it stars Cynthia Erivo, South Africa’s Thabo Rametsi (who plays exiled trumpeter Hugh Masekela) and Guy Pearce. The film tells the story of how Paul Simon and numerous South African artists navigated anti-apartheid boycotts to create the Graceland band and one of the bestselling albums — and most politically significant tours — of the 1980s.

	More to come…

schema.headline: South African President Cyril Ramaphosa Gives Speech at Canal+ Academy Training Program Launch: ‘You Are Living My Dream’

title: Luc Besson Jokes That He Could Make the Next ‘Terminator,’ but Only if the Terminator ‘Sat Down and Said He Missed His Mom’
description:
Luc Besson rejects the idea that he reinvented action cinema. He simply used to have the freedom to experiment.

	“When you don’t have a lot of exp
body:
Luc Besson rejects the idea that he reinvented action cinema. He simply used to have the freedom to experiment.

	“When you don’t have a lot of experience, you have all this freedom. You aren’t controlled by big studios and 50 people telling you why you can’t do something because it costs too much. For about 20 years now, people with money have taken control of cinema. They say: ‘I pay, so I decide.’ No. The one who decides is the creator.”
	

	“When Modigliani wanted to paint women with long necks and black eyes, that’s what he did. We need to take this freedom back because we are simply killing art. We’re turning it into something that can be sold, like yogurt or socks. There are four crucial things in the lives of men and women: Water, air, love and art. Without them, we’re dead.”

	He added, “Now, we have replaced everything with money. And it’s going to kill us all.”

	Besson was speaking at Torino Film Festival, where he received the Stella delle Mole award for lifetime achievement. Earlier that day, he deadpanned, “I saw the list of all the people who have received it, and I didn’t understand why I hadn’t received it too. I’m not used to receiving awards in my own country, so I’m happy to receive one abroad.”

	Celebrated for “The Big Blue,” “Léon: The Professional,” “The Fifth Element” and “Lucy,” Besson was honest about his preferences.

	“Some directors are very good at making films about their neighbors – I don’t know how to do that. I like extraordinary stories. I make films to wander, to disappear and explore other worlds. I don’t want to tell the story of my neighbor. I want to tell the story of a guy who drives a taxi in the 23rd century,” he said, referencing Bruce Willis’ role in “The Fifth Element.”
	

	“These characters are always a little bit broken by society, always on the margins. Also, I like to explore the strength of women and the weakness of men. If I was asked to make another ‘Terminator,’ I’m not interested. I like Schwarzenegger a lot, but I’d only make that film if the Terminator sat down and said he missed his mom.”

	Besson singled out some of the actors he has enjoyed working with the most, from Gary Oldman to ex-spouse Milla Jovovich and star of “Dogman” Caleb Landry Jones.

	“He’s the genius of the decade. He’s a very simple, very sober actor. He doesn’t go out, doesn’t do anything. But when he’s on set, it’s just wonderful. He’ll try everything,” he revealed.

	During the presser, Besson said, “If I could make all my films with [Caleb], that would be fantastic.”

	“As for choosing actors in general, imagine you have to cross the Atlantic in a small boat with just one other person. Choose your partner well, or it will be really hard. Now, I work with actors who are, above all, good people. I don’t want a star surrounded by 15 people.”

	Currently finishing an animated project that he produced and which will be released next year, Besson continues to collaborate with other directors.

	“If someone else could do it as well or better than me, I don’t need to do it myself. I couldn’t have done ‘Taken’ any better. But ‘The Big Blue’ was different. My parents were divers and I spent 15 years studying dolphins, so I wasn’t going to leave that to anyone else. ‘Dogman’ was the same thing. It was a story I was afraid someone else would ruin,” he recalled.

	“Transporter” was another hit for him as a producer.

	“One day, an agent I knew introduced me to a young actor, and I had a drink with Jason Statham. He seemed photogenic. I told him that if I had an idea, I’d call him. I got on a plane and came up with the idea,” he said.

	“We wrote it in a month and financed it in three. Louis Leterrier [who directed with Corey Yuen] was an assistant who wanted to start directing. I asked: ‘Are you ready?’ Hollywood doesn’t know how to do it anymore.”

	Recalling his beginnings, he said, “We were a group of young people who couldn’t get films made because the big studios controlled everything. So we said: ‘Fine, we’ll make them ourselves.’ Suddenly, there were no rules. For 30 years, we did whatever we wanted.”
	

	“Unfortunately, it’s getting harder. That’s a real shame because the films haven’t exactly improved, that’s for sure.”

	Reportedly working on a new sci-fi project, Besson still advocates the kind of cinema that allows people to escape reality.

	“At 14 or 15, I lived far from the city. I could see cows outside of my window, and I felt a strong urge to get away, so I started writing about a taxi pulling up outside my house and taking me off into space. I started writing ‘The Fifth Element’ at 16 because it was my personal way of escaping.”

	“Imagination is a muscle: the more you train it, the stronger it gets. It lets you explore worlds that don’t exist, which is wonderful, because what does exist isn’t that great. Especially right now.”

schema.headline: Luc Besson Jokes That He Could Make the Next ‘Terminator,’ but Only if the Terminator ‘Sat Down and Said He Missed His Mom’

title: ‘Dangal’ Casting Director Mukesh Chhabra Recalls Auditioning Nearly 14,000 Girls, Shares Self-Tape Tips at IFFI Masterclass
description: Mukesh Chhabra, the casting director behind “Dangal” and Shah Rukh Khan‘s upcoming “King,” took aspiring actors and filmmakers behind the scenes of
body:
Mukesh Chhabra, the casting director behind “Dangal” and Shah Rukh Khan‘s upcoming “King,” took aspiring actors and filmmakers behind the scenes of the casting process at a masterclass at the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI) in Goa.

	The session, “The Casting Magic: Auditions Unplugged,” turned into an extended conversation, with participants asking about everything from self-tapes and social media to age and the demands of the profession.
	

	Introducing Chhabra, festival director Ashutosh Gowariker, whose “Lagaan” was nominated for the foreign-language film Oscar, said, “What I like about Mukesh is his eye for character and he will go to any length to find the actors who fit in.”

	Chhabra, whose casting credits include “Dhurandhar,” Aamir Khan’s “Dangal,” Anurag Kashyap’s “Gangs of Wasseypur,” Nitesh Tiwari’s “Ramayana” and “King,” due Dec. 24, described the casting director’s role as a bridge between actors and directors. His work begins with understanding a script and the director’s vision, then determining whether a character calls for an established face or someone new.

	“There is so much talent in our country,” he said. “I send my team all over the country to scout for talent. You have to go to the roots. Our country has so many cultural arts and sub-cultures where so much raw talent is displayed.” Directors, he added, hire him for “my opinion, my ideas, not for my data.”

	The scale of the search can be considerable. For “Dangal,” he recalled auditioning nearly 14,000 girls over almost two years. For “Gangs of Wasseypur,” he cast 384 people. That film, he said, “changed my life.”
	

	Chhabra urged actors preparing for an audition to go beyond memorizing lines and analyze a character’s background, circumstances, social position and motivations. “Designing the scene in your head is important. We want to understand the actor’s intellect. Please do your homework,” he said. “If you understand life, you can understand acting.”

	On self-tapes, his advice was to choose a clean background, ensure good lighting and clear sound, use someone who can deliver cues naturally, and frame the shot close enough to capture the face and eyes. “I want to focus on your face, your performance, not on the painting behind you,” he said.

	Asked about social media influencers moving into acting, Chhabra drew a distinction between performing in self-created videos and interpreting a character in a scripted story. “If you really want to take your job seriously, you have to learn the craft,” he said, recommending theater as a way to build confidence and develop an understanding of performance.

	“It’s a part of your life, you’ve got to deal with it. You chose this profession. If you feel rejected and sad all the time, you will miss a lot of opportunities,” he said of rejection.

	“Acting has nothing to do with age, talent is the only thing,” Chhabra said. He advised performers to keep their appearance simple rather than arrive with a preconceived look for a role.

	He urged actors to stay curious about the world around them. “Read people. Talk to people. Understand people. That’s more important,” he said. “It is all a game of patience and positivity. If it is meant for you, it will come to you.”

	Questions about nepotism and the casting couch brought some humor into the discussion. Chhabra said he had rejected several star kids. “Whether you are a star kid or not a star kid, ultimately you have to act,” he said. Asked about the casting couch, he pointed to his seat on stage. “This is the only couch I like. I’m sitting on it.”

schema.headline: ‘Dangal’ Casting Director Mukesh Chhabra Recalls Auditioning Nearly 14,000 Girls, Shares Self-Tape Tips at IFFI Masterclass

title: ‘High Fidelity’ Director Stephen Frears Still Teases Jack Black: ‘I Told Him, You Owe All This to Me!’
description:
Honored with a lifetime achievement award, director Stephen Frears arrived at the Torino Film Festival in a reflective mood. 

	Over a storied care
body:
Honored with a lifetime achievement award, director Stephen Frears arrived at the Torino Film Festival in a reflective mood. 

	Over a storied career, the British filmmaker embodied the anti-Thatcher counterculture with features like “My Beautiful Laundrette” and “Sammy and Rosie Get Laid,” before earning Oscar glory with dramas such as “Dangerous Liaisons” and “The Queen.” But above all, Frears takes pride in his pop-culture footprint, particularly films “that have found audiences and touched people.” 
	

	Chief among them is “High Fidelity,” his 2000 romantic comedy starring John Cusack, Lisa Bonet and Catherine Zeta-Jones. A famously unfaithful adaptation, the cult classic moved Nick Hornby’s London-set novel to Chicago’s Wicker Park and built a soundtrack that film music aficionados still obsess over. Frears is happy to take some credit for the coup.

	“I always thought it was a very good book, and that it was really about love,” he says, explaining the geographical liberty. Only in crossing the Atlantic, he found a new set of collaborators, steeped in the music that would define the film. “I was very, very lucky. I was already quite old, so I didn’t really know the music,” he says with a laugh. “Everyone who worked on the film knew about music. So I said, ‘I’ll sit over here. You bring me the music, and I’ll tell you if it goes in the film or not!'” 

	Discovering Jack Black was another “stroke of luck.” At the time, Black was known for bit parts in films like “Mars Attacks!” and “Bob Roberts,” as well as his musical comedy duo Tenacious D. His turn as a bombastic music snob in “High Fidelity” catapulted him to leading-man status and cemented a screen persona that has since proved durable and lucrative.
	

	Frears certainly agrees.

	“[In 2003,] he took me to the premiere of ‘School of Rock,'” the filmmaker recalls. “As the lights went down, I told him, ‘You owe all this to me.’ And Jack replied, ‘I know!’ I recently had lunch with him in London, and teased him, asking, ‘Do you have any films that aren’t successful?'”

	Frears followed “High Fidelity” with 2002’s “Dirty Pretty Things,” which, in turn, gave Chiwetel Ejiofor his star-making role. The film tackled the exploitation of undocumented migrants, a subject Frears believes cinema had largely overlooked. “It was the first time a film was made about modern Britain,” he says. “So many people entering the country were illegal immigrants, and this was the first film to address that.”

	Having chronicled Britain under Thatcher and Blair, Frears is just as bleak about the country today. “We’re broke,” he says. “We have no money. You know, it’s all a disaster. So the biggest story today is how to sort that out.” 

	He has little doubt where to place the blame.

	“The people who did Brexit should be in prison,” he says. “These people have destroyed the British economy. Now anybody sensible would like to [get back into Europe], but [the anti-EU people] all still out there making trouble. They’re dreadful, dreadful people. My poor country!”

	“[Brexit] cost about 5 or 6% of our GDP,” he continues. “I mean, it was completely idiotic. You would see these politicians on television talking about sovereignty. Nobody’s interested in sovereignty. We have a queen and a king, so we don’t have to worry about that. What were all the conversations about? I never understood. It was clearly economic ruin.” 

	Until another project crosses his desk (“All I do is read scripts and pick them out,” he says), Frears has been catching up on contemporary releases. Heading home from Turin, he is especially keen to see recent Palme d’Or winner “Fjord.” 

	Indeed, as with Ejiofor and Black, “Fjord” director Cristian Mungiu can thank the Torino honoree for a career milestone. As president of the Cannes jury in 2007, Frears did, after all, award the Romanian filmmaker his first Palme d’Or, for “4 Months, 3 Weeks and 2 Days.”

	“It was a very tough year, with a lot of good films,” Frears recalls. “[‘The Diving Bell and the Butterfly’ director] Julian Schnabel was very cross with me for not giving him the prize. He told me as much!” 
	

	Frears also peeled back the curtain onto that year’s jury deliberations, which famously saw the Coen brothers’ eventual Oscar winner “No Country for Old Men” leave the Croisette empty-handed. “The jury just refused to talk about it,” says Frears, attributing their reticence to “anti-Americanism.” 

	He adds: “But I said, ‘This is the film that people all over the world will actually go see!'”

schema.headline: ‘High Fidelity’ Director Stephen Frears Still Teases Jack Black: ‘I Told Him, You Owe All This to Me!’

title: Barun Sobti, Abhishek Banerjee Star as ‘Paatal Lok’ Creator Sudip Sharma Swaps Violence for Black Comedy in Netflix’s IFFI Selection ‘Pushpak Vimaan’
description: After the crime dramas “Paatal Lok” on Prime Video and “Kohrra” on Netflix, creator Sudip Sharma is changing lanes with “Pushpak Vimaan,” a black c
body:
After the crime dramas “Paatal Lok” on Prime Video and “Kohrra” on Netflix, creator Sudip Sharma is changing lanes with “Pushpak Vimaan,” a black comedy and crime caper starring Jaideep Ahlawat, Abhishek Banerjee and Barun Sobti that is expected on Netflix in early 2027.

	Two episodes of the series screened at the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI) in Goa, after which Sharma, Sobti and Banerjee spoke with Variety.


	“I was just feeling the need to change my lane,” Sharma says. The streaming business, he adds, can keep creators returning to successful shows and their sequels. “Honestly, it wasn’t the plan to be doing only grand dramas. But that’s how life panned out, which is fine. I had real fun doing it. But it felt like I needed to change,” he says. After co-directing the second season of “Kohrra,” he says, “I wanted to just give myself more and newer challenges.”
	

	“I’m a huge fan of the Coen brothers. Black comedy is my favorite comedy genre,” says Sharma, who has long been drawn to crime capers. What he wanted to leave behind was the violence. “It was a very deliberate choice. Because I’ve dealt with a lot of violence,” he says. Rather than build the series around a conventional whodunit, he wanted to introduce the characters and their motivations early and let the audience follow the consequences of their choices.

	Since he was taking on a genre for the first time, Sharma says, he knew he wanted to be surrounded by friends and brothers. “I wanted people who would have my back, and I would have their backs, and just that feeling of trust,” he says.
	

	Ahlawat starred in “Paatal Lok,” as did Banerjee, who played the hammer-wielding killer Hathoda Tyagi and is now Bhaskar, a startup entrepreneur. Sobti, who worked with Sharma on “Kohrra,” plays Bhupi. “I knew I was writing the part for Jaideep, I knew I was writing the part for Barun,” Sharma says.

	When Sobti asked how to approach Bhupi, “‘Just be yourself,’ he told me,” Sobti says. Sharma describes Sobti as “this really awkward, sweet, kind of confused guy,” not unlike Bhupi. “The quality of writing that he pulls off is remarkable and he’s terrific with his casting,” Sobti says of Sharma. “I really hope this show does well for him.”

	“Finally, someone thinks I’m not just a small-town boy who can play quirky or funny parts, or someone who can only play dark, psychotic characters. I was tired of that,” Banerjee says of the role. Sharma wanted him to play the entrepreneur straight rather than join the comic antics, and Banerjee says situational comedy is his favorite because it is about reacting to the other actors, not playing for laughs.

	Sharma describes the Pushpak Vimaan, the flying chariot of the Hindu epic the “Ramayana,” as “that mythical vehicle that can take us from the mess that we are into a place that we want to be in.” His characters, he says, are “all wanting to get away from the morass that they think their life is in, and going for this pot of gold.”

schema.headline: Barun Sobti, Abhishek Banerjee Star as ‘Paatal Lok’ Creator Sudip Sharma Swaps Violence for Black Comedy in Netflix’s IFFI Selection ‘Pushpak Vimaan’

title: Justin Timberlake Was ‘Really Reluctant’ to Make Tell-All Documentary: ‘I’ve Gone Through a Lot in the Last Five Years’
description: Justin Timberlake is opening up about his decision to participate in an upcoming tell-all documentary, saying he was initially “really reluctant.”
body:
Justin Timberlake is opening up about his decision to participate in an upcoming tell-all documentary, saying he was initially “really reluctant.” 

	As Variety first reported, the singer is the subject of “Timberlake,” a four-part documentary from director Fisher Stevens that will premiere on Apple TV Dec. 11. During an appearance on longtime friend Jimmy Fallon’s late-night show on Thursday, Timberlake spoke for the first time about the doc, which sources told Variety delves into the infamous wardrobe malfunction with Janet Jackson and his relationship with Britney Spears.
	

	“I was really reluctant to do it … I think I’m sort of famously private,” Timberlake told Fallon. “I have a relationship with Fisher Stevens, who is a wonderful director and a great human. When Fisher first approached me to do this, I was reluctant, because I was like, ‘I don’t wanna talk about myself,’ you know? But the more we sat down and talked, the more I found myself kind of searching for something that was beneath the surface a little more.”

	Timberlake said that once he eventually agreed, “I sort of mustered up some courage to talk about things that I’ve never talked about before. Things that even those that are closest to me don’t know.”

	He added, “You just never know what somebody’s going through, right? And I think I kind of decided, maybe people see my life from the outside and it’s like, ‘Wow!’ But everybody’s going through something, and I think I’ve gone through a lot in the last five years that I feel like has made me a better human and a better father, a better husband, a better friend.” 
	



	Though Timberlake didn’t detail the documentary’s revelations, he has kept a relatively low-profile since his “Forget Tomorrow” world tour, which concluded last year. During the tour, he announced that he had been recently diagnose with Lyme disease, which had affected his performances. In 2024, he was also arrested for driving while intoxicated in Sag Harbor, New York, and pleaded guilty to a reduced charge of non-criminal driving while ability impaired. It’s likely that both of these topics will also come up in the documentary. 

	“I found the whole experience to be really cathartic,” Timberlake said. “And I hope that when I do share the things that I share in the documentary, that anybody who’s watching it who might have gone through something similar or is just going through anything, can see somebody like myself and sort of feel like, ‘Well, if he can have the courage to speak on it and be vulnerable about it’ … Maybe I can be a beacon of light for whoever’s watching.” 

	Elsewhere during Timberlake’s time on “The Tonight Show,” he and Fallon revisited their viral 2012 “History of Rap” video by performing a “History of Party Songs,” which included “I Want It That Way” by NSYNC’s old rivals the Backstreet Boys. Watch the full video below.

title: The Best Gifts for Gamers in 2026: Consoles, Headsets and the Year’s Buzziest Releases
description: Everyone has a gamer in their life, and the holidays are the perfect time to get them something special, whether it’s a new console, a buzzy title,
body:
Everyone has a gamer in their life, and the holidays are the perfect time to get them something special, whether it’s a new console, a buzzy title, a pair of headphones or an accessory that lets them play on the go.

	Variety has curated this list of the best video game gifts in 2026, so you can surprise your gamer loved ones with the perfect presents this holiday season.

	Shop our list below:




						
			
	

	
					

	Nintendo’s latest upgrade to its flagship console is a crowd-pleaser for all ages. Its modular design means you can play on the TV or in handheld mode, with a bigger, sharper screen than the original Switch. The Switch 2 is perfect for the person in your life who is obsessed with “Super Mario,” “Pokémon” and “The Legend of Zelda.” Some highly anticipated new games are only available on the newest console, while most older Switch games still work on it too.




						
			
	

	
					

	For the gamer who wants Xbox’s huge library without the higher price tag of the Series X, the Xbox Series S is a great option. It’s all-digital and compact enough to fit onto a crowded media shelf. Still, it runs the year’s biggest games, including “Grand Theft Auto VI” and “Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4.” Pair it with a Game Pass subscription and get access to hundreds of titles.



		

						
			
	

	
					
		

										BESTSELLER						

					PlayStation 5		

		
	

	The PlayStation 5 is best for big, blockbuster games, and it’s the console to beat for anyone who loves an interactive cinematic adventure. “Grand Theft Auto VI” landed on the PS5 to near-perfect reviews, and it’s the only console where you can play “Marvel’s Wolverine.” The experience is top-notch down to the controllers, and the deep library spans everything from family-friendly hits to grown-up thrillers.



		

			
			
			
			
	

	
					
		

										NEW RELEASE						

					‘The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time’ Remake		

		
	

	Experience one of the greatest video games ever made, built anew for the Switch 2. Hyrule has never looked this lush, and modern controls and smart updates smooth out the original Nintendo 64 game’s frustrations while keeping every dungeon, side quest and secret intact. You can even play Link’s songs by humming into the console’s microphone. This is the perfect gift for nostalgic “Zelda” fans and newcomers preparing for Nintendo’s upcoming live-action movie.



		

						
			
	

	
					
		

										NEW RELEASE						

					‘Grand Theft Auto VI’		

		
	

	Take part in the cultural phenomenon. Thirteen years after “GTA V,” the most anticipated game of all time is finally here, and critics have deemed it worth the wait. “Grand Theft Auto VI” heads back to Vice City in Rockstar’s sprawling, sun-baked take on Florida. The story follows criminal duo Lucia and Jason, a modern-day Bonnie and Clyde, in a world so detailed it could take you a lifetime to run out of fun discoveries. For the adult gamer on your list — this is definitely no “Mario Party” — no other game comes close this year.



		

						
			
	

	
					
		

										NEW RELEASE						

					‘Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4’		

		
	

	In a return to form, “Call of Duty” has produced the series’ best campaign in years with “Modern Warfare 4.” The new game features a globe-spanning story built around a North Korean invasion of South Korea. The multiplayer game mode lets you play online with friends, and it brings back DMZ, in which squads battle enemies and rival players to escape with their loot. For the first-person shooter fan in your life, this is a sure bet.




						
			
	

	
					

	Every kid with a Wii’s dream vacation spot was Wuhu Island, the tropical resort where you can skydive above the clouds, duel above the ocean and play ping-pong by the beach. “Nintendo Switch Sports Resort” brings back the sunny getaway spot, updating Wuhu Island for the Switch. The game features 12 sports, including golf, bowling, archery and a surprisingly intense thumb-wrestling event, all played with simple motion controls the whole family can learn. This is the ultimate, easy holiday party game for grandparents, kids and everyone in between.




						
			
	

	
					

	Video games exist in everyone’s pocket. And with the 8BitDo FlipPad mobile gaming controller, you can turn your smartphone into a handheld console. The tiny controller has a built-in USB-C connection, which allows you to plug and play any number of mobile games immediately. This is the perfect affordable gift for a gamer who likes to play on the go.




						
			
	

	
					

	What’s old is new again. Vinyl, VHS and now the Evercade Nexus, a retro gaming system built around curated cartridges of classic games, with no downloads, subscriptions or online accounts required. This bundle includes a cartridge with “Banjo-Kazooie” and “Banjo-Tooie,” two of the most beloved 3D platformers from the 1990s. Play the Nexus on the go or on the TV and grow your collection of cartridges from a library of more than 700 classic games, from “Metal Slug” to “Earthworm Jim.” It’s simple enough for kids and pure nostalgia for their parents, which makes it a gift the whole household can share.




						
			
	

	
					

	Excited about the announcement that Robert Pattinson is the next James Bond? Go deeper into the spy franchise with “007 First Light,” a brand-new origin story from the makers of the “Hitman” games. The game follows a young Bond from his early days in the Navy to his first missions with MI6. It plays like a movie you can control, with sneaky spycraft, car chases and explosive set pieces across luxurious locations. Lana Del Rey even wrote the theme song!




						
			
	

	
					

	One of the best-selling video game franchises in the world is back with another installment, and “Mario Kart World” is its biggest iteration yet. Instead of separate tracks, the game’s courses are stitched into one giant world you can drive across without stopping, almost like an open-world game. Plus, each race now holds 24 racers, which means twice the red shells and banana peels. The standout game mode is Knockout Tour, a marathon race where players are eliminated at each checkpoint until one champion remains. This game is perfect for the whole family, so fire up the engines and pray you don’t get blue shelled.




						
			
	

	
					

	A PlayStation 5 exclusive, “Marvel’s Wolverine” hails from Insomniac, the studio behind the hit “Spider-Man” games. “Wolverine” is a full superhero blockbuster, and it’s much darker and bloodier than “Spider-Man.” The game’s story finds Logan clawing his way through the mystery of his own past, and the controller rumbles with every grisly slash. For PS5 owners, this is one of the year’s must-have games.




						
			
	

	
					

	Imagine “Animal Crossing,” but with Pokémon. In “Pokémon Pokopia,” you can rebuild a ruined world into a paradise for Pokémon — where they can live, farm, craft and just vibe. There are no battles to stress over, just a relaxing routine of gardening, building and making new friends. This game is certainly not for your action junkie friend, but it is the cozy pick of the year, a surprise hit that was well-liked by critics.


		

						
			
	

	
					
		

										BESTSELLER						

					‘Grand Theft Auto VI: The Album’		

		
	

	For the “Grand Theft Auto” fan who can’t get enough of its soundtrack, this vinyl bundle has 34 original tracks inspired by the game’s neon-soaked Vice City. Artists include Dua Lipa, Lana Del Rey, Travis Scott, SZA, Justice, Tame Impala, Burna Boy, Jennie, Morgan Wallen and Keith Richards. Pressed on two transparent magenta discs with blue splatter, the records look as good on the shelf as they sounds on the turntable.



						
			
	

	
					

	For gamers who like to talk to their friends while playing — or just like to soak up the sound with a good pair of headphones — the HyperX Cloud III is the solid, budget-friendly pick. They’re wired, which means no batteries are necessary, and it plugs into every console. And controls sit on the ear cup for easy volume and mic modification.

title: Chiwetel Ejiofor Was Afraid to Make ‘Backrooms’ Because of Director Kane Parsons’ Age: ‘He Was So Young!’
description:
Chiwetel Ejiofor had his doubts when he was first approached to make the hit horror film “Backrooms.”

	Directed by Kane Parsons, a YouTuber-turned
body:
Chiwetel Ejiofor had his doubts when he was first approached to make the hit horror film “Backrooms.”

	Directed by Kane Parsons, a YouTuber-turned-director, the film was produced for $10 million and has already surpassed $400 million at the global box office, becoming one of the most profitable movies of the year.

	“When I was told that Kane was only 19 years old when I was first sent the script, I thought it was very strange. He was so young! I guess I was thinking of myself at that age, and I wondered if it was plausible. Then I saw his web series [‘Backrooms’] and it was incredible. I thought it was absolutely brilliant,” he said during a press conference at Torino Film Festival.
	

	In the film, Ejiofor plays a furniture store owner who discovers a mysterious portal into another dimension. Variety’s Owen Gleiberman called it a “creepy meditative dada horror trip in the what-is-reality? tradition of ‘Eraserhead’ and ‘Skinamarink.’”

	“I feel like there’s a new generation of filmmakers,” continued Ejiofor. “They have a lot of online access, which means that a lot of the ideas are also pressure-tested. There are people who watch it and [they are] in the comments section. People aren’t shy about telling you their opinions and thoughts.”

	He added: “With Kane being able to communicate with millions of people and have his work interact with that number of [viewers], he was able to really refine his work in a way that wasn’t possible a generation ago. We didn’t have that sort of forum or access to people watching our work. He made a lot of it in his basement at home!”
	

	“Obsession,” made by 26-year-old Curry Barker, was another monster hit: it has made $516 million globally.

	“It’s a very exciting time for young filmmakers and for a whole new wave of talent. I think that, in the next few years, we’ll get to see a lot from this generation,” said Ejiofor.

	While still best known for award-winning dramas like “12 Years a Slave,” he has always wanted to “explore cinema.” Apart from “Backrooms,” this ambition led him to the Marvel Cinematic Universe, where he played Karl Mordo in “Doctor Strange” and “Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness.”

	“I was thrilled to join that,” he said.

	“I’ve always wanted to do lots of different kinds of films in my career, lots of different genres, different characters, different styles of films. I think it’s because that’s how I am as an audience member. I love watching all sorts of films,” he said.

	“I enjoyed being in Marvel films, the scale and the size of them, their reach and their fan base. It continues to expand in ways that, even 10 years ago, I don’t think we expected.”

	There’s just one thing he asks for as an actor: his characters need to evolve.

	“It moves me. One of the hardest things for people to do is to truly change and change their inner qualities. Sometimes very epic things have to happen for this to occur. There has to be large amounts of drama, wars and conflict.”

	He said: “I find it moving when I see characters who are in pursuit of that. In pursuit of change or growth in some way. And that’s the kind of thing that, again, can happen across any genre.”

title: RECLab 2026: New Films From ‘Alcarràs,’ ‘Romería’ Producers Bound for a Key New Spanish Talent Forum
description: Lluis Segura’s AI title “Electrónica,” as well as “Mother of Sugar” and “La Unión,” from the producers of “Alcarràs” and “Romería” respectively, bi
body:
Lluis Segura’s AI title “Electrónica,” as well as “Mother of Sugar” and “La Unión,” from the producers of “Alcarràs” and “Romería” respectively, bid fair to be potential standouts at the 12th edition of Primer Test, the industry centerpiece of RECLab, one of Spain’s most important new directorial talent labs.

	Part of the RECTarragona Film Festival, which takes place Dec. 2-8, REC Lab, directed by Javier García Puerto, unspools over Dec. 3-6 in Tarragona. 
	

	A 75-minute drive south of Barcelona, it sources projects from Catalonia and its vibrant arthouse scene. Producers of Primer Test titles take in some of the foremost Catalan industry figures including Tono Folguera (“Alcarràs”), Àngels Masclans (“Romería”), Ariadna Dot (a producer on TIFF Fipresci Award winner “Forastera” and Platform laureate “They Will Be Dust”) and Mireia Graells Vivancos (behind SXSW hit “Fury”).

	At least five of the seven titles, to be screened in post-production as works in progress, are feature debuts for their directors, however.

	They will hope for as much success as titles sneak-peaked at RECLab in the past as a important testing ground such as Cannes’ 2023 Directors’ Fortnight Best European Film winner “Creatura” and “Mamífera,” a SXSW Best Performance Special Jury Prize winner for María Rodríguez Soto.

	Establiliz Urresola’s “20,000 Species of Bees,” the Berlin Festival 2023 Best Performance winner, was the first victor at RECLab’s Screening Test, before its Berlin selection. How the film should end was decided after that Screening Test.
	

	“Electrónica,” from Barcelona’s ESCAC film school, J.A. Bayona’s alma mater, marks “an ambitious visual experiment,” says director Lluis Segura, “making AI not just the subject of its story, but an integral part of its cinematic language.”

	A RECLab 2026 buzz title, “Mother of Sugar” weighs in as a landmark project for Spanish cinema, led by Andrea Álvarez, an actress with an intellectual disability, producer Adriana Dot told Variety.

	The biggest international co-production at RECLab, “La Unión”marks the latest from Àngels Masclans, a producer on Carla Simon’s well received 2024 Cannes Competition contender “Romería.”

	“Off Season” reps the feature debut of Marta Font, a director on Netflix hit Spanish series “Intimacy” which was led by “Money Heist” star Itziar Ituño.

	Primer Test titles also takes in “Juliette & Camille,” from Paloma Zapata, director of international sales breakout “La Singla.” “Mirage” marks Santa Cecilia and producer Marieta Caballero Baeza’s feature debut; Mauricio S. Burckhardt’s “Another Wreck,” won three of the four post-production awards at Colombia’s Cartagena Film Festival, one an invite to RECLab.

	Some titles are well-known. “La Unión,” for instance, was developed at the ECAM Madrid Film School, TorinoFilmLab and Bogotá Audiovisual Market, among other programs. “Electrónica,” by contrast, has flown under the radar. “Juliette & Camille” has been put through nine development programs including Málaga’s MAFF, Guadalajara’s Co-Production Meeting and Sanfic Industria.

	Women near double men as the directors or lead producers of Primer Test titles, a sign of the robust driving force behind so much of the now near decade-old Newest Catalan Cinema – think Carla Simón, Meritxell Colell or Pilar Palomero – which grew out of films grounded in a sense of place but addressing universal issues.

	Immigration figures prominently at Primer Test. Both “La Unión” and “Another Wreck” focus on the consequences of relocation decades later in the present day, but are inspired by the directors’ real family story of migration. In “Another Wreck,” the director’s own family archive from World War II is woven into the fiction.
	

	“Off Season” is a “family reconnection drama,” noted producer Mireia Graells. As is “La Unión.” Many of titles capture the contemporary search for identity. Bedrock relationships can be found, however, beyond those of a cisgender couple or biological family. 

	“Juliette & Camille,” for instance, marks a search for belonging, framed as a relationship to place and intimacy with chosen people in a world in flux. “Without belonging, you’re left with a deep sense of solitude,” says Camille, French but now settled in Galicia.

	A closer look at Primer Test titles:

	“Another Wreck,” (“Otro Naufragio,” Mauricio S. Burckhardt, Haus Kino, Colombia, Bam Bam Cinema, Portugal)

	Silvia receives an old suitcase filled with letters, photographic rolls and clothes, buys a used book and, within its pages, finds a letter in German which mentions a hotel. She goes there and stays a night. “A Nouvelle Vague-inflected romance set in present-day Bogotá,” says Burckhardt from Haus Kino, whose “Meteorite” premiered at Venice Intl. Film Critics’ Week. The feature debut of Burckhardt who directed Colombian TV series “Of Love and Other Misfortunes.”



	

					‘Another Wreck’
	



	“Electrónica,” (Lluis Segura, ESCAC, Spain)

	One of the most intriguing projects at this year’s RECLab, produced by the evergreen Sergi Casamitjana, head of ESCAC. Max, an electronic music composer, is obsessed with creating music that changes the world. Then a follower, Z3nith, sends him the design of a neural device capable of rewriting the mind. “Blending live-action footage with AI-generated worlds,” but still “a deeply human story about love, obsession and the illusion of control,” Segura told Variety.

	“Juliette & Camille,” (Paloma Zapata, La Fabrica Naranja, Spain, Indígena Films, both Spain; Boca del Cielo Producciones, México)

	Juliette, born in Barcelona to Peruvian parents and searching for her roots, meets up with electronic music specialist Camille, who crates songs drawn from the sounds of nature. They set out to make together a song over three rainy days at a sound studio in a forest in Galicia. As the song grows, their relationship flowers.“Juliette & Camille” is “a universal story about identity, memory, the transformational power of artistic creation, said producer Sara Horta.
	



	

					‘Juliette & Camille’
	



	“Mirage,” (Pablo Santa Cecilia, produced by Marieta Caballero, Spain)

	Paris, 2014. Anna and Chiara, a couple, film their daily life. 2017: a homophobic attack leaves Chiara dead. Years later, two friends set out to make a documentary about them from hundreds of home videos; “reality and fiction starts to dissolve into a feverish dreamscape of grief,” says the synopsis. “My intention is to explore that ambiguous space between reality and fiction, giving the audience the freedom to decide what ‘Mirage’ is,” says Santa Cecilia.



	

					‘Mirage’
	



	“Mother of Sugar,” (“Mare de sucre,” Clàudia Cedó, Lastor Media, Suica Films, Deliris Films, Spain)

	María, 35 years old, with 65% intellectual disability, cherishes a lifelong, deeply held desire to become a mother. When challenged, she decides to reclaim control over her body and future and stop asking for permission. Based on Cedó’s Goya-nominated short 2023 “De sucre” and produced by Tono Folguera’s Lastor Media, Ariadna Dot’s Deliris Films and Rafa Moles’ Suica Films, “an intimate, human story with a powerful contemporary question about autonomy, desire and freedom,” says Dot.



	

					‘Mother of Sugar’
	



	“Off Season,” (“Temporada Baixa,” Marta Font, Ringo Media, Spain)

	At a beach, a widower and his two children face an autumn of changes, silences and uncertainty, until one night reunites them, ending the off-season. A film about “three people of different ages each facing their own personal crisis,” says Font.

	Starring Quim Avila (“Ravalear”), from Mireia Graell Vivancos’ Barcelona-based Ringo Media, behind Berlin-selected “Matria,” and two SXSW premieres: “My Sextortion Diary” and “Fury.”



	

					‘Off Season’
									Roser Vilagrassa
	



	“La Unión,” (Cordelia Alegre, Dos Soles Media, Wknd, El Sol Ermitaño, Rara Cine, EFD, Spain, Colombia)

	After their mother’s death, Cecilia and Juliana, 19-year-old twins, travel for Christmas to Colombia, where they were born but barely remember. Cecilia delves into their father’s past and Juliana struggles to understand her own present. Born by Alegre’s “personal journey to reconstruct her mother’s and aunt’s story, exploring how we build bonds with people we have never met and the silences that shape our identities,” says producer Angels Masclans.



	

					‘La Unión’

title: Florida Thanksgiving Feast Leaves 18 Sick, 15 Hospitalized

                          15 Hospitalized After Suspected Food Poisoning

                                  November 26, 2026
                                4:35 PM PST
                                    
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
              A Thanksgiving feast in Florida turned into a holiday nightmare ... with 18 people falling ill from suspected food poisoning and at least 15 landing in the hospital.
      
    
              The dinner disaster unfolded Wednesday at Leon Medical Centers' headquarters in Doral, near Miami, where employees gathered for an early Thanksgiving celebration.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
              But the holiday cheer didn't last long ... several staffers began experiencing gastrointestinal symptoms after the catered meal, prompting a massive emergency response.
      

              According to Miami-Dade Fire Rescue, 18 people reported feeling sick, with 15 initially transported to hospitals. The situation was serious enough for officials to declare a Level 3 mass casualty incident.
      
    
              Leon Medical Centers confirmed an outside catering company provided the food and says it's working to determine what went wrong ... stressing that no patients were affected.
      
    
              Safe to say ... nobody's asking for seconds.

title: Venomous Sea Snakes Washing Ashore on Southern California Beaches, Officials Warn
description:
California Beaches
                          Venomous Snakes Washing Ashore
body:
California Beaches
                          Venomous Snakes Washing Ashore
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              November 26, 2026
                            5:00 PM PST
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  November 26, 2026
                                5:37 PM PST
                                    
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
              California beachgoers might want to watch where they step ... 'cause venomous sea snakes are washing ashore ... and experts warn more could be on the way.
      
    
              A yellow-bellied sea snake was discovered Sunday at Bolsa Chica State Beach in Orange County ... marking just the eighth documented sighting of the rare reptile in Southern California.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
              And here's the kicker ... scientists believe unusually warm waters from El Niño are pushing the tropical snakes farther north, meaning this slithery surprise might not be the last.
      

              Researchers at the Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County say high tides through Sunday could bring more snakes onto beaches, with additional sightings possible in early and late December .
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
              Despite their dangerous venom, the snakes aren't typically aggressive toward humans. Still, officials are warning beachgoers to keep their hands off ... advising anyone who spots one to snap a photo from a safe distance and alert lifeguards.
      
    
              So, if you're hitting the beach this holiday weekend ... keep your eyes on the sand ... you never know what might wash up.

title: Thanksgiving Earthquake Hits Off Baja California Coast, Magnitude 5.7
description:
Thanksgiving Shake-Up
                          5.7 Quake Strikes Off Baja Coast
body:
Thanksgiving Shake-Up
                          5.7 Quake Strikes Off Baja Coast
                      
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
              A magnitude 5.7 earthquake struck a remote group of islands off Mexico's Baja California peninsula on Thanksgiving ... delivering a holiday shake-up in the Pacific Ocean.
      
    
              The quake hit Thursday near the Revillagigedo Islands, roughly 216 miles from Cabo San Lucas, at a depth of about 6 miles.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
              Fortunately, the remote location means the earthquake is unlikely to affect many people ... though it's unclear whether any aftershocks could strike closer to the mainland ... and the region was already rattled by a magnitude 4.2 earthquake just one day earlier.
      

              The Revillagigedo Islands are volcanic and federally protected by Mexico, boasting such a rich marine ecosystem that National Geographic has dubbed them the "Galápagos of Mexico."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
              The Thanksgiving tremor comes just days after back-to-back earthquakes shook Southern California's beach cities ... including a magnitude 3.2 quake in Orange County early Monday and a magnitude 3.3 quake off Manhattan Beach on Sunday.
      
    
              Mexico also experienced a magnitude 4.7 earthquake in Baja California earlier this month.
      
    
              For now, it appears the holiday got off to a shaky start, with no major destruction.
